content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, 'justify/justification' is understood as a forensic (legal/courtroom) term meaning to be declared righteous before God — the act by which God acquits the sinner and counts or reckons that person righteous, on the basis of faith in Jesus Christ rather than works of the law. In classic Protestant formulation this is a declarative act in which Christ's righteousness is imputed to the believer (justification by grace alone through faith alone). It is contrasted with condemnation and treated as the reversal of the guilty verdict, grounded in Christ's atoning death and resurrection.", "primary_basis": ["Romans 3:21-28 (justified freely by his grace through the redemption in Christ Jesus; justified by faith apart from works of the law)", "Romans 4:1-8, 4:25 (Abraham believed God and it was counted to him as righteousness; raised for our justification)", "Romans 5:1 (therefore, being justified by faith, we have peace with God)", "Romans 5:9, 5:16-19 (justified by his blood; the one act of righteousness leads to justification and life)", "Romans 8:30, 8:33 (whom he called he also justified; it is God who justifies)", "Galatians 2:16 (a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ)", "Galatians 3:6-14, 3:24 (justified by faith; the law as guardian until Christ)", "Genesis 15:6 (Abraham believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness — cited in Romans 4 and Galatians 3)", "Habakkuk 2:4 (the righteous shall live by faith — cited in Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11)", "Philippians 3:9 (not having a righteousness of my own from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ)", "Titus 3:5-7 (justified by his grace, not by works done in righteousness)", "2 Corinthians 5:21 (that we might become the righteousness of God in him)", "Luke 18:9-14 (the tax collector went home justified rather than the Pharisee)"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Roman Catholic (Tridentine) view: justification is not merely a declaration but an actual making-righteous — an infusion of grace that inwardly transforms and sanctifies the person, beginning at baptism and increasing through faith working in love and cooperation with grace; it encompasses what Protestants distinguish as sanctification.", "basis": ["Council of Trent, Decree on Justification (1547)", "James 2:14-26 (a person is justified by works and not by faith alone)", "Galatians 5:6 (faith working through love)", "Romans 2:6-13 (the doers of the law will be justified)", "1 Corinthians 6:11 (you were washed, sanctified, justified)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "New Perspective on Paul (Sanders, Dunn, N.T. Wright): justification is primarily a covenantal/ecclesiological declaration — God's verdict that one is a member of his covenant people — and Paul's polemic against 'works of the law' targets Jewish boundary markers (circumcision, food laws, Sabbath) rather than merit-seeking legalism; final justification is rendered in accordance with the whole life lived.", "basis": ["Romans 3:29-30 (God of Jews and Gentiles alike)", "Galatians 2:11-16 in its table-fellowship context", "Romans 2:13 and 2 Corinthians 5:10 (future judgment according to works)", "E.P. Sanders, Paul and Palestinian Judaism (1977); J.D.G. Dunn; N.T. Wright, Justification (2009)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Eastern Orthodox reading: justification is not a discrete forensic category but part of the single process of salvation as healing and union with God (theosis); the West's legal framing is regarded as foreign to the patristic Greek understanding of dikaioō as being made righteous through participation in Christ.", "basis": ["2 Peter 1:4 (partakers of the divine nature)", "John 15:1-11 and 17:20-23 (abiding/union texts)", "Patristic tradition (e.g., Athanasius, Cyril of Alexandria, Maximus the Confessor)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "James's 'demonstrative' sense: in James 2:14-26, 'justified' means shown or proved to be righteous — vindicated by works as the evidence of genuine faith — a usage most Protestant interpreters harmonize with Paul by distinguishing declarative from demonstrative justification.", "basis": ["James 2:21-25 (Abraham and Rahab justified by works)", "Matthew 11:19 / Luke 7:35 (wisdom is justified by her deeds/children)", "Luke 7:29 (the people justified God, i.e., acknowledged him righteous)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Justification as participation/union with Christ rather than (or prior to) imputation: righteousness is received through incorporation into Christ, so that the believer shares his vindicated status; associated with apocalyptic and participationist readings of Paul (Schweitzer, Sanders, Campbell) and with the Finnish Lutheran school's reading of Luther (justification as Christ's real presence in faith).", "basis": ["2 Corinthians 5:17-21", "Philippians 3:8-9 ('found in him')", "Galatians 2:19-20 (crucified with Christ; Christ lives in me)", "Romans 6:1-11 (union with Christ in death and resurrection)"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "'Faith of Christ' (pistis Christou) subjective-genitive reading: believers are justified by the faithfulness of Jesus Christ (his obedient faithfulness unto death) rather than, or logically prior to, their own act of believing; shifts the ground of justification from human faith to Christ's fidelity.", "basis": ["Galatians 2:16, 2:20; 3:22", "Romans 3:22, 3:26", "Philippians 3:9", "Richard B. Hays, The Faith of Jesus Christ (1983)"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Ecumenical convergence view: justification is God's gracious act by which sinners are both declared and made righteous, forgiveness and renewal held together; represented by the Lutheran–Catholic Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999), which treats the declarative and transformative aspects as inseparable.", "basis": ["Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999)", "Romans 3:23-25; 5:1; 1 Corinthians 1:30"], "prominence": "minority"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "Unlike many symbolic terms, 'justification' is a technical theological term rather than an image or emblem, so 'symbolic meaning' here amounts to its doctrinal sense. There is broad consensus across traditions that it concerns being set right/righteous before God through Christ; the sharp and historic division is over the mechanism and nature of that act — forensic declaration with imputed righteousness (classic Protestant, dominant in evangelical and Reformed teaching), versus transformative infusion (Roman Catholic), versus covenantal-membership verdict (New Perspective), versus healing/participation (Orthodox). The Protestant forensic reading is presented above as primary because it is the most widely recognized default in English-language biblical-studies and popular Christian teaching contexts, but the Catholic transformative view is equally official within the world's largest Christian communion, so 'settled consensus' applies to the general meaning, not to the disputed mechanics."}
